name: Barhadbeshabba 'Arbaia
knownFor: Bishop of Halwan in the Church of the East who wrote the Cause of the Foundation of the Schools. Addai Scher calls it the first history of the school of Nisibis, whose masters it names from Narsai of Nisibis to the author's own master, Henana of Adiabene.
dates: No source used here gives the year of his birth or death. Addai Scher dates the Cause after Ishoyahb of Arzun became head of the church, which Scher puts in 581, and before 604. R. H. Connolly puts it a little after 585, and a note by the editors of the Patrologia Orientalis about 590. A Bar Hadbeshabba, bishop of Halwan, signs the acts of the synod of Gregory of Prat, which J.-B. Chabot dates to April 605. A chronicle Ignazio Guidi edited names him in the vacancy after Gregory's death, which François Nau and Scher give as 609 to 628. Scher thinks he probably died in the first half of the seventh century
place: Beth 'Arbaye by origin, as his epithet shows, Addai Scher says, a place Joseph Assemani puts in the diocese of Nisibis; the school of Nisibis, in the Persian empire; Halwan, which the synod's acts spell Holwan, as bishop
tradition: The Church of the East under Persia
role: Student of the school of Nisibis; bishop of Halwan; writer of the Cause of the Foundation of the Schools

keyWorks.title: Cause of the Foundation of the Schools
keyWorks.about: the schools through which God taught angels and people, from Adam to the apostles and the schools of Alexandria and Antioch, ending with the schools of Edessa and Nisibis and the masters of Nisibis down to Henana of Adiabene. A note by the editors of the Patrologia Orientalis reads it as an opening address for the school session

keyWorks.title: History of the Holy Fathers Persecuted for the Truth (the Ecclesiastical History)
keyWorks.about: in its held second part, lives of Theodore of Mopsuestia and Nestorius, the Council of Ephesus, and the Nisibis teachers Narsai and Abraham. François Nau gives it to Barhadbeshabba 'Arbaia, priest of the school of Nisibis, and thinks it not impossible that he is the bishop of Halwan

traces: Addai Scher calls the Cause's account of the schools of Edessa and Nisibis very precious, the first work to trace the history of the school of Nisibis. Since it was written at the end of the sixth century, he trusts it over later accounts on Narsai's forty-five years at Nisibis and on Elisha, Narsai's successor, never being a bishop.
R. H. Connolly calls the part of it that Alphonsus Mingana first printed of first-rate importance for the history of the school of Nisibis. He reckons Narsai's death from its forty-five years.
François Nau says the History seems to be the oldest church history of the Church of the East, that all later writers used it, and that it is the source of the Syriac legend of Nestorius.
remembered: An anonymous chronicle that Ignazio Guidi edited says that in the years after Gregory of Prat died, Bar Hadbeshabba of Halwan won fame for writing books.
J. Labourt calls Barhadbeshabba of Holwan a distinguished writer.

Abdisho of Nisibis lists books of a Barhadbeshabba 'Arbaia: the Treasures in three volumes, controversies against all sects, a church history, a work on the followers of Diodore, and a commentary on Mark and David.

uncertain: His own life is thin in the sources. It rests on the title and words of the Cause, a signature in the synod of 605, a line in the Chronicle of Seert and one in the chronicle Guidi edited. Addai Scher joins all of these to one man. François Nau joins the signature and Guidi's chronicle to the Cause's author.
The signer. The acts of 605 list a Bar Hadbeshabba, bishop of Holwan, without the epithet 'Arbaia. Scher and Nau take him to be the Cause's author, whose title calls him bishop of Halwan.

Bishop or metropolitan. The synod's acts and the Cause's title call him bishop. The Chronicle of Seert says a Hadbeshabba 'Arbaya was made metropolitan of Houlwan; Scher reads the name as Barhadbeshabba.

The History and the Cause. Nau gives the History to Barhadbeshabba 'Arbaia, priest and head of the overseers of the school of Nisibis by its title, the writer Abdisho of Nisibis lists. He thinks it not impossible that this man is the bishop of Halwan, who would then have written the History young and the Cause in old age. Scher treats them as one, giving the Cause's author Abdisho's list of books. He notes that Abdisho's list does not name the Cause.

When the Cause was written. Scher dates it between Ishoyahb of Arzun's rise and 604, from the events it tells and the walk-out. R. H. Connolly puts it a little after 585, the year he gives for Henana's condemnation. The editors of the Patrologia Orientalis say about 590.

His part with Henana. The Cause praises Henana as a living master and calls the troubles against him the devil's work. Scher thinks the author probably hid the truth to praise his master, since Henana's church always charged him with leaving Theodore of Mopsuestia. The Chronicle of Seert puts a Hadbeshabba 'Arbaya among the students who left the school in protest. Scher asks why the pupil would leave the master he praised, and guesses he followed the stronger party. He also suggests the Cause was written to bring peace back to the school.

The Cause's worth. Scher reports that Alphonsus Mingana took it for part of Barhadbeshabba's history, and that J.-B. Chabot judged it a poorly joined set of older accounts. Scher holds it a separate work to be trusted fully. He thinks the passages that troubled Chabot, found in Mingana's manuscript, were added by a copyist.
The line in Guidi's chronicle. In Guidi's Latin, Bar Hadbeshabba of Holwan won fame for writing books, and others of the time stood out for their way of life. Nau's French gives him both.

Namesakes. The Chronicle of Seert and Mari ibn Sulayman name a Barhadbeshabba, monk of Mount Sa'ran, whom Sabrisho wanted as his successor; J. Labourt thinks the bishop of Holwan is perhaps that man. Joseph Assemani thinks Abdisho's Barhadbeshabba a different man from the one who lived in the time of Jacob, founder of the monastery of Beth Abe. Others are the deacon Barhadbeshabba of Arbela, Barhadbeshabba of Qardu, and the archimandrite Bar Hadbeshabba to whom Ishoyahb III wrote.
